tagline: Home of the highest mountains on Earth
overview:
Nepal is wedged between India and China along the spine of the Himalayas, a rectangle of land about the size of Arkansas that climbs from steamy lowland jungle to the summit of Mount Everest in less than 200 kilometers. Eight of the world's fourteen mountains above 8,000 meters stand wholly or partly inside its borders.

About 30 million people live in Nepal, speaking Nepali as the national language along with more than 100 others. Kathmandu, the capital, fills a green valley ringed by peaks, its old squares crowded with pagoda-roofed temples, brick palaces and shrines where pigeons, monks and motorbikes share the same courtyard.

Nepal was a kingdom for more than 200 years and became a federal republic in 2008. Most Nepalis are Hindu, with a large Buddhist minority; the Buddha was born at Lumbini in the southern plains. Farming terraces, tourism and the work of Nepalis abroad support much of the country.
landAndNature: Nepal has three stacked worlds. The Terai in the south is flat, hot and fertile, part of the Ganges plain. Above it rise the green middle hills, carved into stepped terraces where rice and millet grow. Higher still stand the Himalayas, including Everest at 8,849 meters, Kanchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Annapurna and Manaslu. Rivers born of glaciers cut gorges deeper than any in the world; the Kali Gandaki runs between two 8,000-meter giants. Chitwan and Bardiya national parks in the lowlands protect one-horned rhinos, Bengal tigers, gharial crocodiles and wild elephants. Snow leopards and red pandas live in the high forests, and the danphe, a rainbow-colored pheasant, is the national bird.
peopleAndCulture: Nepal is a mosaic of peoples: Newars in the Kathmandu Valley, Sherpas and Tamangs in the mountains, Magars, Gurungs, Tharus, Madhesis and many more. Dal bhat, lentil soup over rice with vegetable curry and pickles, is eaten twice a day by most families, and momo dumplings are the favorite snack. Festivals fill the calendar: Dashain, the longest, brings families home for two weeks, and Tihar honors crows, dogs and cows on separate days. The national sport is volleyball, though cricket and soccer draw big crowds. Sherpa climbers are the backbone of Everest expeditions, and Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit with Edmund Hillary in 1953. Nepal's flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle.
history: The Kathmandu Valley has been settled for more than 2,000 years, and Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini around the 500s BC. Newar kings built the valley's three rival royal cities, Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, filling them with carved wooden temples. In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered the valley and united Nepal. British armies fought the Gorkhas to a standstill in 1814–1816 and afterward began recruiting Gurkha soldiers, who still serve in the British and Indian armies. Nepal was never colonized. The Rana family ruled as hereditary prime ministers from 1846 until 1951. A Maoist insurgency from 1996 to 2006 killed thousands, and in 2008 parliament abolished the monarchy. A huge earthquake in 2015 killed about 9,000 people and toppled historic temples.
funFacts: Nepal's flag is the world's only non-rectangular national flag, made of two stacked triangles bearing a moon and a sun.
Nepal keeps its clocks 5 hours and 45 minutes ahead of London, an offset shared with no other country.
Mount Everest grows a few millimeters taller each year as the Indian plate keeps pushing into Asia.
There is no New Year's Day in January here: the official Bikram Sambat calendar is about 57 years ahead and starts in April.
Kathmandu's Boudhanath is one of the largest stupas in the world, with painted eyes looking out in four directions.
